links.outcome: Clinician perceptions of accountability and liability for AI-assisted decisions
links.effect: Clinicians felt ultimately liable for patient outcomes yet relied on AI-generated insights, raising questions about liability if systems malfunctioned.
links.quote: Nevertheless, accountability surfaced as a pervasive concern: while clinicians felt ultimately liable for patient outcomes, they also relied on AI-generated insights, prompting questions about liability if systems malfunctioned.

links.outcome: Clinician trust in opaque black-box AI models lacking interpretability
links.effect: Clinicians emphasized difficulty trusting black box models lacking clear rationale or interpretability, particularly for rare or complex cases.
links.quote: Transparency emerged as another major theme, with clinicians emphasizing the difficulty of trusting “black box” models that lack clear rationale or interpretability—particularly for rare or complex cases.

links.outcome: Reported AI underperformance in minority patient groups or atypical presentations
links.effect: Bias was repeatedly cited, especially when algorithms underperformed in minority patient groups or in identifying atypical presentations (qualitative reports, no quantified metrics).
links.quote: Bias was repeatedly cited, especially when algorithms underperformed in minority patient groups or in identifying atypical presentations.

screen.reason: Qualitative study examining healthcare professionals' perspectives on accountability, transparency, and bias in AI-assisted decision making.
